parameters.description: A tenant id or slug. `404 org_not_found` when it matches neither, so a typo is not read as "no events".

parameters.name: actor
parameters.description: A user id, or an email (case-insensitive, exact).

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: An exact action (`member.invite`), or a prefix ending in `*` (`provider.*`).

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Only events at or after this instant. Epoch milliseconds or an ISO-8601 date.

200.description: One page of tenant audit events.

404.description: `org_not_found`: the `org` filter matched no tenant id or slug.

get.summary: List the platform operators' own audit trail
get.description:
`platform_audit_events`, newest first: every mutating `/api/platform` request (written after
the handler ran, so `status` is the real response), and every refusal of a token that
carried the `platform-operator` role (`result: denied`, `action: platform.access.denied`,
`metadata.reason` naming the failed check). Reads are not recorded unless the handler is
itself sensitive, so an operator browsing the console leaves no rows.

`last_24h` counts rows per result over the last 24 hours across the WHOLE table, whatever
the filters - it does not change as you page.

parameters.name: actor
parameters.description: The token subject (`actor_sub`), or an email (case-insensitive, exact).

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: An exact action (`platform.access.denied`), or a prefix ending in `*`.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The acted-on object's identifier, exact.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Only events at or after this instant. Epoch milliseconds or an ISO-8601 date.

200.description: One page of operator audit events, plus the 24-hour counts.

get.summary: Every runtime flag, its effective value and where it came from
get.description:
Reads nothing destructive and is not audited. `effective` is the decision the worker is
making right now: a boolean for an `enabled` flag, the parsed integer for
`PROVIDER_BUILD_MAX_QUEUED`.

`source` says which layer won — `override` (a row), `env` (the deploy) or `unset` (neither,
so the registered default applies). `env_value` is always reported so an operator can see
what removing the override would give them, which is the question they actually have.

200.description: Every registered flag, in registry order.

brakes_engaged.description: Brakes whose effective value is `false` — i.e. something is stopped.

propagation_seconds.description:
The isolate cache TTL. A change is in force everywhere within this many
seconds; until then some isolates still hold the previous value.

put.description:
Writes the override row. `value` is the **raw string**, parsed exactly as the env var is, so
`"0"` and `"1"` keep their meanings — and for `PROVIDER_BUILD_MAX_QUEUED`, `""` means the
default of 15 while `"0"` means dispatch nothing. That distinction is why the column is TEXT
and why this takes a string rather than a boolean.

**`reason` is required.** A brake with no reason is one nobody dares lift later, because the
person who set it is the only one who knows what it was for. It is recorded on the row and
in the audit event.

**A value the flag's own parser would reject is refused** with 400 `bad_value`. A boolean
flag takes only `"0"` or `"1"`: `"true"`, `"yes"` and `"on"` all read as OFF through a
`!== '1'` gate, so accepting them would leave an operator believing they had enabled
something.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The env var's own name, e.g. `PROVIDER_BUILD_ENABLED`.

value.description: The raw value, as the env var would carry it.

reason.description: Why. Required, and recorded on the row and in the audit event.

example.reason: Build fleet is starving Authentik; holding dispatch while the quota is resized.

200.description: The flag as it now resolves.

400.description:
Invalid JSON, a missing `value` or `reason`, or `bad_value` — the value is not one the
flag's parser accepts.

404.description:
`unknown_flag` — the name is not in the registry, so no code reads it. The response
lists the names that are, because the usual cause is a typo. Nothing is written: a row
for an unread name would look like a brake and do nothing.

delete.summary: Remove an override, reverting to the deployed value
delete.description:
Deletes the override row. The flag goes back to its env var — which is why the response
carries the flag's new resolution rather than just a confirmation.

**Answers 200 whether or not there was a row to delete**, with `removed` saying which. "There
is no override" is the state the caller asked for, not a failure, and an operator clearing a
brake during an incident should not have to care whether someone else got there first.

200.description: The flag as it now resolves, and whether a row was removed.

404.description: `unknown_flag` — the name is not in the registry.

get.summary: Scan/build pipeline health for the operator console
get.description:
One call for the Fleet page: queue-supervisor heartbeats per queue kind, non-terminal rows
by table and status, stuck-row counts per reaper arm, module/state/plan scan attempts over
the last 24 hours, provider job outcomes over the same window, dead-lettered provider jobs,
and the derived flow state of in-flight provider jobs.

A heartbeat row that is `present: false` means the supervisor has never reported for that
queue kind; the reapers' lost-message arms stand down for it. `fresh` uses the same rule
as `readWorkflowObserver`, so it is exactly what the reaper sees.

Stuck counts list every arm, zero included, so the page can say what was checked. The
`*_undispatched` arms are the lost-message arms: they only reap while that kind's
heartbeat is fresh and not at capacity, and stop at the 24h pending deadline so no row is
counted twice.

The flow sample is the oldest `sample_per_kind` in-flight jobs per kind; `truncated` says
more exist. A stale snapshot derives `unknown`, never `queued`.

The rows behind the summary's `stuck` counts, oldest first. Keyset-paginated: pass back
`next_cursor` as `cursor`. A malformed cursor restarts from the beginning rather than
erroring. Normally empty: the reapers fail these rows every 15 minutes, so a standing
list means the cron is not running or a reaper is throwing.

parameters.name: arm
parameters.description: Restrict to one reaper arm.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Page size, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

get.summary: Provider jobs failed by the dead-letter consumer
get.description:
Provider build and scan jobs whose `error_message` is exactly the DLQ consumer's message
(lib/deadLetter.ts): the queue supervisor exhausted its retries and the message went to
the provider-build or provider-scan DLQ. Newest first, keyset-paginated. Module, state and
plan scans have no DLQ handler, so they never appear here.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Page size, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

get.summary: List API tokens across every org
get.description:
Every bot token (`machine_clients` row), with what it can reach. `scope` is derived the way
`TokenService.listByOrg` derives it: `global` when `is_global = 1`, else `state_workspaces`
when the token has any state grant, else `org`.

A `global` token is granted write in EVERY org (rbacTenant's `is_global = 1` arm), and
since 2026-10-21 only a platform operator may create one — through the `post` on this same
path, the only route that can. A global token has `tenant: null` by design (TokenService
stores `tenant_id` NULL for it), and `?scope=global` is how an operator finds the id to
revoke or rotate.

`last_used_at` was never written before the 2026-10-21 fix (auth.ts updated a column that
does not exist), so `null` on an older token does not mean it is unused.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Only tokens of this scope. Absent or empty means all.

200.description: One page of tokens, plus whole-table counts by scope.

post.summary: Mint a global-scope API token
post.description:
**The only route that can create a global-scope token.** A global token authenticates as
write in every org — rbacTenant admits it through its `is_global = 1` arm without consulting
membership — so POST /api/orgs/:orgId/tokens refuses `scope: global` (403
`platform_operator_required`) and `TokenService.createGlobal`, which this route alone calls,
is the only code that writes `is_global = 1`. Mint one for cross-tenant automation (a
scanner, a migration run), not for a person.

**`client_secret` is in the 201 body and nowhere else.** The Worker never stores it:
`machine_clients` has no secret column and the IdP will not read one back. An operator who
loses it has no recovery but `/rotate`, which invalidates the old one.

The token belongs to no org, so `tenant_id` is `null`, and `include_modules` /
`include_state` are `null` as well — those narrow an *org* token's reach, and a `none`
there would read as a restriction nothing enforces.

`404 not_found` is about the operator, not the token: `machine_clients.created_by`
references `users(id)`, and the row is created when a human signs in to the portal. An
operator admitted by `PLATFORM_OPERATOR_SUBS` who has never signed in has no user row, so
the fix is to sign in to the portal once. `502 idp_unavailable` means the IdP refused to
create the service account — nothing was written, so retrying is safe.

Audited as `platform.token.create` on `token`; the row records the name and the
IdP client id, never the secret.

example.name: fleet-rescan-2026-10
example.description: One-off cross-tenant rescan after the extraction fix

201.description: The token, with its secret, shown this once.

400.description: Invalid JSON, or `name` is missing or blank.

example.message: `name` is required

404.description: The operator has no `users` row yet — sign in to the portal once.

example.message: User not registered

delete.description:
Deletes the IdP credential first and the `machine_clients` row second. That order is
deliberate: dropping the row first would leave a credential that still authenticates as
write in every org and that no console can see or revoke.

Only a global token can be addressed here — the lookup pins `is_global = 1`, so an org
token's id is a `404` and this route cannot become a cross-tenant delete of any token by
id. Revoking a token that is already gone is also a `404`, which is the normal answer to a
retried revoke rather than a problem.

`502 idp_unavailable` means the IdP refused the delete; the row is left in place on
purpose, so the token stays visible and the revoke can be retried.

Audited as `platform.token.delete` on `token`. The audit row carries the token's
name, read before the delete, because afterwards there is nothing left to name it.

200.description: Revoked. The credential no longer authenticates.

404.description: No global token with this id — it never existed, is already revoked, or is an org token.

example.message: Global token not found

post.summary: Replace a global token's secret
post.description:
Mints a new secret at the IdP and invalidates the old one, keeping the same token id and
`oidc_client_id` — so whatever uses the token changes one value, not its identity. The new
secret is returned once, like a create.

Rotation is the only recovery for a leaked or lost global secret, and the old secret stops
working the moment this returns, so a caller holding it will start failing immediately.

`404` covers two cases the message tells apart: no global token with this id (as on the
delete), or a row with no `oidc_app_id` — one created before that column existed, whose IdP
side cannot be reached. Such a row can only be removed, and the IdP credential cleaned up
by hand; `/machine-clients?issue=missing_app_id` lists them.

Audited as `platform.token.rotate` on `token`.

200.description: The new secret, shown this once.

client_secret.description: The new secret. Never stored by the Worker; `/rotate` again is the only way to get another.

404.description: No global token with this id, or it has no IdP app id to rotate.

no_app_id.summary: Predates the IdP app id column

value.message: Token has no app ID - cannot rotate

get.description:
The same `machine_clients` rows as `/tokens`, viewed from the IdP side: the IdP client and
application ids, rotation and last use, and whether the row has a problem.

`issues` names each problem the row has:
- `missing_app_id` - no IdP application id (rows predating the column), so revoke and
  rotate cannot reach the IdP; removing it is a manual IdP job;
- `tenant_deleted` - the org is soft-deleted but the client, and its IdP credential, remain;
- `never_used` - no recorded use. See the `last_used_at` caveat on `/tokens`.

`oidc_client_id` and `oidc_app_id` are identifiers, not secrets.

get.description:
Every `vcs_repo_trust` row. A trusted subject lets a GitHub Actions / GitLab CI OIDC token
write state and modules for the org with no stored secret, so a wildcard subject
(`is_wildcard`, the subject contains `*`) trusts every repo it matches, not one.

tenants.description: Distinct orgs with at least one trust entry.

get.description:
Users newest first, each with every org membership (active and soft-left). One person can
be several users: each IdP account signs in as its own row, keyed by email.

`sub_is_not_email` flags a user whose stored token subject is not their email. Portal
tokens have carried `sub` = email since the 2026-10-07 claims change and `POST /api/auth/me`
re-keys `oidc_sub` on the next sign-in, so the flag means "has not signed in since then".

Every `form_submissions` row. One table holds the in-app support / beta-feedback form
(name and email from the session) AND the public terramantle.dev contact, founding-member
and enterprise-quote forms (name and email typed by the visitor, so untrusted). The row
does not record which form it came from.

The enterprise quote form stores its structured answers as a JSON string in `use_case`;
`metadata` is that string parsed, and `null` for free text.

Every `feature_interest` row: one per (user, feature), deduplicated on write, so a count is
a count of distinct users. Any signed-in user can record any feature slug, so unknown slugs
appear here even though only a fixed list emails the admin inbox (routes/interest.ts).

`summary.by_feature` ranks every feature (up to 200) by users, ignoring `feature`.

parameters.description: Only rows for this exact feature slug.

Users by creation time, each with the orgs they are an active member of. A signup is the
`users` row `POST /api/auth/me` creates on first sign-in; a new user with no org is given
one, which shows as `auto_created` (an owner membership within 60 s of the signup).

`summary.quiet_after_day_one` counts users with no authenticated request more than a day
after they signed up - people who looked once and did not come back.

get.description:
The checks the console can run, with what a finding means and what to do about it. Runs
nothing and reads no data, so it is not audited.

post.summary: Run one data-integrity check, or all of them
post.description:
Runs the named check, or every check when `check` is omitted. Any row a check returns is a
finding; a check that returns none passes.

**Sequential, not parallel or batched.** D1 executes one query at a time per database, so
parallel checks would only queue behind each other and in front of live traffic, and a
batch is one transaction where a single failing check would discard every result. Each
check runs on its own; one that errors (for example a table missing from this database) is
reported with `status: error` and does not hide the others.

**Time budget.** A D1 query may run for up to 30s and Cloudflare closes a proxied request at
100s, so a full run stops *starting* checks after 60s and reports the rest as
`status: skipped`. Run those one at a time.

**Rows are capped.** At most 50 rows per check come back. Every check also carries its own
`LIMIT` (50 today); `at_limit: true` means the query hit that limit, so there are at least
that many findings and possibly more — read it as "50 or more", not "50".

Audited: the run is written to `platform_audit_events` as `platform.integrity.run`, with
the check name (`*` for all) as the target and the summary counts in the metadata. An
unknown check name is audited too, as `refused`.

parameters.name: check
parameters.description: The check name (a `scripts/integrity/*.sql` file name without `.sql`). Omit to run every check.

200.description: The run, one result per check that was selected.

404.description: No check has that name. `error` is `unknown_check`; `message` is for humans and not stable.

example.message: No integrity check named not_a_check

get.description:
The history, plus whichever operation currently holds the execution slot, plus whether the
worker is armed at all. A read: not audited.

`active` is non-null when something is queued or running. Because only one operation may
hold the slot, a non-null `active` is also the reason an apply would 409.

200.description: The history and the current state.

armed.description: Whether PLATFORM_DESTRUCTIVE_ENABLED is set on this worker.

confirmation.description: The exact text each kind requires, so the console never guesses it.

get.summary: One operation, with the full plan it was approved against
get.description:
Returns the operation and the complete inventory stored at plan time. After a wipe this is
the ONLY record of what was there before, so it is kept verbatim and never pruned.

plan.description: The inventory and volatile snapshot captured at plan time.

404.description: No such operation.

post.summary: Plan the complete removal of one provider
post.description:
Inventories everything a wipe would delete and everything it would keep, and returns a hash
to approve it with. Deletes nothing.

**What a wipe removes:** every provider scan job, result and finding; the global scan cache;
every build job with its overrides and gate verdicts; the auto-patch lineage; the served
version rows; every org's policy results, overrides, entitlements, serve overrides and
download events; the artefact rows; the source urls and latest-version rows; and the derived
`module_provider_refs` and `workspace_providers` references, which are recreated on the next
lockfile or module ingest.

**What it KEEPS, and why:** `provider_build_blocklist`, because a safety record must outlive
the artefact it blocks — a wipe that cleared it would re-admit the thing somebody blocked.
`policies`, `policy_instance_overrides` and `audit_events`, because those are the customer's
own configuration and history, not ours to delete. All four are counted in `kept` so the
operator can see what survives.

**Objects go before rows,** and that ordering cannot be swapped: the D1 rows are the only
index of which objects exist, so deleting rows first turns the bytes into garbage nobody can
ever find. The plan therefore also collects the keys the rows explicitly reference —
pre-migration-111 layouts and case variants are not under any prefix this code knows, so a
prefix sweep alone would silently leave them.

**`blast_radius` is the number the operator is actually reading.** Row counts cannot tell
them whether this provider is dead weight or something three customers pull hourly, so the
plan names the orgs serving it and who downloaded it in the last seven days.

Fork repositories are listed for manual removal: this does not touch GitHub.

201.description: The plan. Nothing has been deleted.

400.description:
Invalid JSON, or an unsafe identity segment. The identity goes into SQL literals and
object-store prefixes, so it is validated against the provider-build-key pattern and
rejected if it contains `..` — this is the check that stops a wipe of `aws` becoming a
wipe of everything beginning "aws".

post.summary: Plan the removal of EVERY provider scan and build record
post.description:
Platform-wide, with no target. Inventories the eight scan and build tables, collects every
SBOM and source-bundle key, and checks the preconditions. Deletes nothing.

**The preconditions are the whole safety story,** and they are reported at the top level so
an operator sees them before typing a confirmation rather than after: builds held at
`PROVIDER_BUILD_MAX_QUEUED = 0`, `PROVIDER_SCAN_DRAIN_ENABLED` off, the auto-patch cron off,
and zero in-flight work. They are checked here, again at apply, and again on every slice —
not as belt-and-braces, but because a purge takes several slices and a scan that starts
mid-run writes rows into tables already emptied, producing exactly the orphan the integrity
checks hunt for. In-flight work is the one gate with no override: those jobs have to finish
or be released, because a job that reports after its rows are gone recreates a fragment of
the set being purged.

**What survives:** tenants, entitlements, the blocklist and yank governance tables, policies
and audit history. A purge clears the scan/build working set, not the platform's decisions
about what may be served.

`patched_provider_versions.build_job_id` is set to NULL as part of the run, before the exit
checks, because a revision pointing at a deleted job is precisely what
`patched_build_job_missing` flags — the purge would otherwise fail its own criterion. The
run is not finished until `patched_build_job_missing` and `scan_job_orphan_rule` come back
clean.

201.description: The plan, including the preconditions that will gate the apply.

get.summary: Soft-deleted orgs, and whether their 30-day window has closed
get.description:
**This is the list that makes a promise keepable.** Deleting an org through the portal only
soft-deletes it (`tenants.deleted_at`) and emails its owners "data will be permanently
removed on <date>", where the date is `deleted_at + 30 days`. Nothing has ever done the
removing — so that promise has been made every time an org was deleted and kept zero times.

`eligible` means the window has closed, so the purge is **overdue** rather than merely
permitted. `reason` says why one is not eligible: `within_promise_window` (the customer was
given a date and it has not arrived), `not_deleted`, `personal` or `demo`.

A read: not audited.

200.description: Every soft-deleted org, newest deletion first.

slug.description: Also the typed confirmation for this org's purge.

eligible_at.description: When the promise window closes. This is the date the owners were emailed.

post.summary: Plan the permanent removal of a deleted org
post.description:
Inventories everything an org purge would delete. Deletes nothing, and is allowed while the
org is still **inside** its promise window so an operator can see what is pending — the
apply is what refuses.

**Scope: 46 tables, derived from the schema rather than hand-written.** 20 reach a tenant
directly by `tenant_id`/`org_id`; the rest through a parent chain up to four levels deep
(`download_events` → `module_versions` → `modules` → tenant). They are deleted children
first and WITHOUT relying on `ON DELETE CASCADE`, because only 11 of the 20 declare it and
whether SQLite enforces foreign keys at all depends on the session.

**Objects before rows, and the reason is sharper here than for a provider wipe:** there is
no per-org prefix in any of the four object layouts, so the rows naming them are the *only*
index of those objects. Delete the rows first and the bytes are unreachable for ever. The
four key sets — module archives, state versions and plan renders (`MODULES_BUCKET`), and
published policy bundles (`POLICY_BUNDLES`, a different binding) — are all read out of the
rows at plan time.

**The tenant row goes last**, because while it exists the org is still findable, which is
what lets a resumed slice locate its own leftovers.

**`platform_audit_events` is never touched.** The operator's own record of having done this
has to outlive its target.

The plan hash covers the org identity, its eligibility, which tables are non-empty and the
exact object keys — but NOT the row counts. A soft-deleted org is mostly inert, yet a
retention prune can still move a count, and that must not withdraw approval. Eligibility IS
hashed: if the org were somehow restored between plan and apply, the approval dies with it.

201.description: The plan. Nothing has been deleted.

confirmation_required.description:
The org's **slug**. The operation's target is the slug rather than the org id
precisely because a uuid cannot be retyped from the screen without copy-paste,
and copy-paste defeats the purpose of typing it. Every query uses the id from
the plan.

inventory.description:
Row counts for all 46 tables, the four object key sets, the member count, and
the org's identity and deletion time.

eligibility.description:
Surfaced at the top level because it is what will refuse the apply — and
`within_promise_window` is the one refusal with no override anywhere in the
system.

400.description: Invalid JSON or a missing `org_id`.

404.description: No such org.

post.summary: Approve and start a planned destructive operation
post.description:
Answers **202**: the work runs as queued slices, not in this request. Poll
`GET /api/platform/operations/{id}` for `phase` and `status`.

Every refusal has its own status, because an operator mid-incident needs to know which thing
to go and fix:

| Condition | Status | Code |
|---|---|---|
| not armed, or paused | 423 | `not_armed` |
| `auth_time` older than 10 min, or absent | 401 | `reauth_required` |
| not in `planned` status | 409 | `conflict` |
| planned against another environment | 409 | `conflict` |
| plan older than 10 minutes | 410 | `plan_expired` |
| wrong or missing confirmation text | 400 | `bad_request` |
| stable fields changed | 409 | `plan_stale`, with `volatile_diff` |
| in-flight work, or purge preconditions unmet | 409 | `conflict`, with `gates` |
| org still inside its 30-day promise window | 409 | `conflict`, with `gates` |
| org no longer exists | 409 | `conflict` |
| another operation holds the slot | 409 | `conflict`, with `active` |

410 rather than 409 for an expired plan is deliberate: the plan existed and no longer
applies, so the fix is to re-plan rather than to retry. 423 rather than 403 for an unarmed
worker is also deliberate: the capability is shut, which is a different problem from this
request being wrong, and is fixed somewhere else entirely.

A successful apply still reports `volatile_diff` — what moved between plan and apply without
withdrawing consent. That is information the operator should have, not a reason to stop.

plan_hash.description: Exactly the hash from the plan response.

202.description: Queued. The operation now holds the execution slot.

queued.description:
False when the queue binding is absent: the operation stays visibly queued
rather than silently never running.

400.description: Invalid JSON, a missing `plan_hash`, or the wrong confirmation text.

401.description:
`reauth_required` — the token's `auth_time` is older than ten minutes or absent. The
response carries `auth_time_present` so the console can tell "sign in again" apart from
"this IdP never emits the claim, so the step-up can never be satisfied".

404.description: No such operation.

409.description:
A conflict. `plan_stale` carries `planned_hash`, `current_hash` and `volatile_diff`;
an unmet precondition carries `gates`; a contended slot carries `active`.

410.description: `plan_expired` — the plan is older than ten minutes. Make a new one.

423.description:
`not_armed` — PLATFORM_DESTRUCTIVE_ENABLED is unset (a deploy-time decision) or
PLATFORM_DESTRUCTIVE_PAUSED is engaged (liftable on the Brakes page).

post.summary: Stop a planned, queued or running operation
post.description:
Marks the operation cancelled and frees the execution slot.

**A running operation is marked, not interrupted.** Nothing can stop an invocation
mid-flight, so the in-flight slice finishes what it is doing and no further slice starts —
every slice re-reads the status before acting, which is what makes this work at all. The
response says so explicitly, because "cancelled" appearing instantly while deletes continue
for a few more seconds is otherwise alarming.

Whatever was already deleted stays deleted. A cancel is not a rollback; there is no rollback.

404.description: No such operation.

post.summary: Continue an incomplete or failed operation from its saved phase
post.description:
Re-queues the operation, keeping its phase and cursor, so it carries on rather than starting
again. Every phase is idempotent, which is what makes this safe: deleting an already-deleted
key and deleting from an already-empty table are both no-ops.

**The confirmation is required again.** Resume continues an irreversible operation whose
plan was approved against a world that has by definition changed — the first run deleted
things. The step-up applies too.

Only an `incomplete` or `failed` operation can be resumed, and only when no other operation
holds the slot.

400.description: Invalid JSON or the wrong confirmation text.

401.description: `reauth_required` — the step-up applies to a resume as well.

404.description: No such operation.

409.description: Not resumable, or another operation is active.

get.summary: Headline platform counts for the operator console
get.description:
The console's landing figures. Counts only, with no thresholds applied: whether a
heartbeat is stale or a job is stuck is the fleet endpoint's call, since it imports the
reapers' own constants.

Tenant figures exclude soft-deleted orgs; demo orgs are counted separately so `active`
means real customers. In-flight builds use the schema's own in-flight set
(`pending`, `building`, `signing`, `publishing`); in-flight scans are `pending` or
`processing`. Every timestamp is epoch milliseconds.

get.summary: One org's policy bundle pointer, drift check and policies
get.description:
`bundle.drift` is `true` when the stored pointer's revision is not what the policy rows
hash to now - an edit not yet republished (the rebuild queue or the hourly reconciler
catches up), or a publish that keeps failing. `bundle.stored_object` is `false` when the
pointer names an R2 object that is missing; OPA then 404s on this org's bundle and the
gate fails closed. It is `null` when bundle storage is not configured. `bundle` is `null`
for an org that has never published.

A policy's `snapshots` are its Rego as it was before each change (an edit, or an
automatic `pre_v1_syntax` / `pre_v2_contract` rewrite), newest first. Rego itself is not
in this response; download it with the routes below.

200.description: The pointer, the drift check and every policy, enabled or not.

404.description: No such tenant.

get.summary: Download one org's OPA policy bundle
get.description:
Default: the stored object the pointer names, byte for byte what OPA pulls. With
`rebuild=1`: the bundle assembled from the policy rows now, never written anywhere.
Diffing the two answers "is the gate running stale policy". Audited.

404.description:
`not_found` (no such tenant), `no_bundle` (never published), or
`bundle_object_missing` - the pointer is ahead of its object, which means OPA is
getting a 404 for this org right now.

503.description: Bundle storage is not configured on this deployment.

get.summary: Download every policy's authored Rego for one org
get.description:
Every policy as authored - packages NOT relocated, disabled policies included, neither of
which the bundle ships - laid out `<slug>/<artefact_type>/<baseline|custom/<instance>>/
<name>-<id>.rego`, with each policy's snapshots under `<slug>/snapshots/` and an
`<slug>/index.json` describing every file. Audited.

404.description: No such tenant.

get.summary: Download one policy's Rego, or one of its snapshots
get.description:
The policy's current Rego as authored, or with `snapshot` the Rego as it was before the
change that snapshot precedes. The policy must belong to the tenant in the path. Audited.

parameters.name: snapshot
parameters.description: A snapshot id from `GET /api/platform/tenants/{tenantId}/policy`.

404.description: No such policy in this tenant, or no such snapshot of it.

get.description:
Default: the object the published pointer names, exactly as OPA pulls it. Unlike the
internal route OPA uses, a missing object is a `404 bundle_object_missing` here rather
than a silent inline rebuild - the internal route hides that case to keep OPA ready, an
operator needs to see it. `rebuild=1` builds one from the mirrors now; its revision moves
only when the facts do (`generated_at` is excluded from the hash).

404.description: `no_bundle` (never published) or `bundle_object_missing`.

503.description: Bundle storage is not configured on this deployment.

get.summary: Download the reference document as built from D1 now
get.description:
The document a policy reads as `data.terramantle.ref` - `kev`, `epss` (only at or above
`epss_floor`; absence below it means "below", not "unknown"), `aliases`, `licenses`,
`generated_at`. Built now, so it is what the next publish would contain;
`X-Bundle-Revision` is the revision that publish would carry.

get.summary: Download the reference projection scan pods receive
get.description:
The same lean projection `GET /internal/reference-data` gives a scan pod: `kev` as an
ARRAY of CVE ids (the shape the deployed scanners parse), `aliases`, and the timestamps.

get.summary: Download the KEV mirror as CSV
get.description:
Every CVE the mirror flags as known-exploited, newest addition first, with EPSS where
known. Columns: `cve_id,kev_added,kev_due,known_ransomware,epss,epss_at,updated_at`.
`updated_at` is the sweep that last confirmed the row; because a sweep clears every KEV
row it did not touch, a row lagging the others means the clear itself did not run.

get.summary: Download the KEV mirror as JSON
get.description: The same rows as `kev.csv`, as `{generated_at, count, items}`; timestamps are epoch ms.
The discovery bundle OPA polls - one `config/data.json` naming every org bundle and the reference bundle.

get.summary: Download the (tenant, revision) index the discovery bundle is built from
get.description:
`bundles` is every org's current `(tenant, revision)`; `reference` is the reference
bundle pointer, or `null` before its first publish. An org missing from `bundles` has
never published, so OPA holds no bundle for it.

get.summary: Policy bundle, reference data and CVE mirror freshness
get.description:
One answer to "is the policy machinery current?", from four independent sources:

- **Org bundles** (`policy_bundle_revisions`). Every org with a published bundle OR at least
  one enabled policy, worst first. `behind` = published against a policy-input contract older
  than `current_contract_version`; `PolicyBundleService.resolveQueryPath` refuses such a
  bundle, so that org's gate fails CLOSED until it is republished. `missing` = enabled
  policies and nothing published, which also fails closed. Orgs with neither are left out:
  they have no gate to be stale. `items` pages through this list; `bundles` counts the
  whole set.
- **Reference bundle** (`policy_reference_bundle`). `generated_at` moves only when the
  content changed - an unchanged publish is skipped - so it is "last content change", not
  "last checked". `null` before the first publish.
- **CVE mirror** (`cve_intel`). `kev_swept_at` is the OLDEST `updated_at` among KEV rows: a
  sweep stamps every row it writes with one timestamp, and `MAX(updated_at)` would be moved
  by the EPSS refresh on its own.
- **Rego snapshots** (`policy_rego_snapshots`): append-only copies taken before a rego
  change, grouped by reason (`edit`, `pre_v1_syntax`, `pre_v2_contract`).

`stale` flags mean older than `stale_after_ms` (48h: the reference cron runs daily).

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The previous response's `next_cursor`, verbatim. `400` if it was not issued by this endpoint.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Orgs per page. Values above 200 are clamped to 200.

200.description: The freshness report, with one page of orgs.

get.description:
The provider-status report: the scan queue (marker rows in `provider_version_scans`),
scan and build jobs by status with 1h/24h completions and stale/stuck counts, 24h timings
and top failures, patched revisions by status, and hourly completions over the last 24
hours.

Each query fails on its own. A failed section comes back empty and its error is in
`errors` keyed by section, as the script reports it, so one bad query does not blank the
page; an empty `errors` object means every section is real.

`argo` cross-checks D1's in-flight jobs against live provider Workflows, as the script does
with kubectl. With `ok: false` (`not_configured`, `unreachable`, `http_<n>`) the two lists
are empty because nothing was checked, not because nothing is wrong.

get.summary: Outstanding scan and build work, per provider version
get.description:
Every distinct provider@version the platform knows about (artefact versions plus scan-cache
rows with no artefact behind them, such as `self_built` lineages), with a scan state and a
build state derived by the drain's and reaper's own thresholds. Not org-scoped: a version
managed by three orgs is one unit of work, and `orgs` counts them.

`build-due` is a candidate the auto-patch scheduler would consider, not one it will build
this tick: the scheduler also applies an eligibility filter (newest majors, references)
that this view does not reproduce. `never-built` is the unbuildable remainder (not
scanned, a non-registry lineage, or past the attempt cap) and is not counted as
outstanding.

`totals` and `providers` describe the whole filtered set, not the page, so they stay
fixed while paging. Items are ordered provider, newest version first, then upstream.
Cloudflare queue depth is not included: the worker has no analytics credential for it
(the script reads it with CF_API_TOKEN).

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: Restrict to one provider, `<namespace>/<type>`.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Keep versions whose scan OR build state is this.

parameters.name: outstanding
parameters.description: `1` keeps only versions with actionable work (scan backlog, build-due, build-failed).

200.description: One page of the backlog, with totals for the whole filtered set.

get.summary: Provider build jobs across every org
get.description:
`provider_build_jobs`, newest first, keyset-paginated (pass `next_cursor` back as
`cursor`; a malformed cursor is a `400`). Each row's `flow` is derived from the pushed
snapshot only - no Argo call per row - so an in-flight row with a stale snapshot reads
`unknown`, never `queued`. The detail route fetches the live Workflow.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: A job status, or `inflight` for pending, building, signing and publishing.

parameters.name: via
parameters.description: `requested_via`, e.g. `manual` or `scan`. The column is free text.

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: `<namespace>/<type>`.

get.summary: One provider build job, with its Workflow
get.description:
The job row, its gate verdicts and overrides, the patched revision it produced, and its
flow. While the job is in flight the flow comes from a live Argo read; once terminal, from
the Workflow archive by `workflow_uid`. Either read failing leaves `flow` on the pushed
snapshot and says why in `argo`.

`gate_verdicts` is EMPTY for a blocked build (`flow.blocked: true`): the gate-runner
reports a block as the Workflow's failure, not as verdict rows. Read the reason from the
CR named in `argo_cr`.

get.summary: Provider scan jobs across every org
get.description:
`provider_scan_jobs`, newest first, keyset-paginated like `/builds`. `org: null` is a
platform-scoped scan (an auto-patch patched-tree scan), not a missing org. `flow` is
snapshot-only.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: A job status, or `inflight` for pending and processing.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: `full` scans the artefact; `cve_refresh` re-matches stored SBOMs against current CVE data.

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: `<namespace>/<type>`.

get.summary: One provider scan job, with its results and Workflow

post.summary: Yank a self-built provider version
post.description:
Stops serving the self-built bytes for ONE lineage — the `{upstream}` in the path. The
terraform.io and opentofu.org revisions of a provider may share a version string and still
be different bytes, so yanking one deliberately leaves the other served.

This was an org-admin action until it moved here. It is not a tenant's decision: the rows
it marks carry no org, so a yank stops the version being served to *every* entitled org.

**Yank is not a recall.** A consumer that already has the hash in its lock file keeps
resolving the version; what changes is that a NEW `terraform`/`tofu init` gets
`not_found`. To refuse a version even for pinned consumers, blocklist it.

`yanked_rows: 0` with `200` is the ordinary answer when nothing self-built is cached for
that version — nothing was being served, so nothing had to stop. It is not an error, and
it is not a "no such version" either: this endpoint never claims the version exists.

A `reason` is optional (it defaults to `yanked by platform operator`) because the audit
row already names the operator and a yank is recoverable by rebuilding.

Audited as `platform.provider.yank` in `platform_audit_events`, target
`{upstream}/{namespace}/{type}/{version}`, with the affected row count in the metadata.

reason.description: Recorded in `yank_reason` on the rows this marks, and in the audit metadata.

200.description: Yanked. `yanked_rows` is how many cached revision rows changed, possibly zero.

400.description:
The path does not name a provider version: `upstream` is not terraform.io or
opentofu.org, `namespace`/`type` are not `[a-z0-9-]+`, or `version` is not a version
string. Same checks, same messages, as the retired org route. Audited as `refused`.

post.summary: Blocklist a provider version (the undo-malware kill switch)
post.description:
Hard-fails a `(namespace, type, version)` — the version STRING, in **every** lineage. The
`{upstream}` in the path only validates the path here; the kill switch is deliberately
global, because malware does not respect which registry a tree was built from.

**This is the one action that reaches already-pinned consumers.** The resolver refuses any
blocklisted tuple, so a lock-file consumer's re-resolution breaks loudly instead of
silently re-downloading the bytes. Together with out-of-band key revocation it is the only
true undo-malware path — a pinned hash cannot be quietly recalled. That blast radius is
why this is an operator action and not, as it once was, an org admin's.

Blocklisting also yanks every self-built row for the version, so it does not resolve for a
new init either.

**`reason` is mandatory.** The row IS the incident-response record, and a blocklist with no
stated cause is one nobody can safely lift later. It is stored truncated to 1000
characters (and to 500 in the derived `yank_reason`).

**Idempotent, and quietly so.** The blocklist is unique per
`(namespace, type, version)`, so re-blocklisting an already-blocked version answers `200`
and keeps the FIRST reason — the later call's reason survives only in the audit row. There
is no un-blocklist endpoint: lifting a kill switch is a deliberate out-of-band act.

Audited as `platform.provider.blocklist` in `platform_audit_events`, target
`{namespace}/{type}/{version}` with no lineage, since no single lineage was blocked.

reason.description: Why the version is being refused. Kept as the incident record.

example.reason: malware confirmed in the vendored tree (INC-1421)

200.description:
Blocklisted, or already was. No row counts: the blocklist is a single row and the
yank it implies covers every lineage, so counting them would only invite the reader to
treat zero as a failure.

400.description:
A malformed path (as for yank), or no `reason`. Audited as `refused` either way, so a
refused kill switch still leaves a trace of who tried.

example.message: `reason` is required for a blocklist (incident-response record)

get.summary: Whether the console can see telemetry, and why not
get.description:
Calls Grafana's `/api/health`, the one endpoint that proves the tunnel, CF Access and the
bearer all work without reading anyone's data. Also returns the pinned datasource UIDs and
the caps, so the console does not hard-code either.

`configured: false` means `GRAFANA_API_URL` or `GRAFANA_API_TOKEN` is unset on the worker.
`configured: true, reachable: false` means they are set and the call failed — `reason`
carries `unreachable` (timeout) or `http_<status>` (Grafana refused). A 403 upstream means
the Viewer SA was denied; a 502 means Grafana itself errored.

Answers 200 in every one of those cases: this endpoint reports the health of the telemetry
path, so a broken path is its 200 answer, not its error.

post.summary: Run a LogQL query against Loki
post.description:
`query_range` over Loki, capped at 24h and 500 lines.

**The stream selector must pin an exact label.** Every `{...}` selector in the expression
needs an exact `=` match on `service_name`, `namespace` or `job`, and a selector that does
not have one is refused with 400 `bad_expression`. Loki reads every stream a selector
admits, so `{namespace=~".+"}` is a cluster-wide scan wearing a filter's clothes; one exact
matcher lands the query on a single service's streams, which is what a console panel wants.
Every selector is checked, not just the first — otherwise `{service_name="a"} or {}` would
smuggle an unbounded read past a guard that stopped at the first match.

Worker logs are the exception worth knowing: they exist only under
`{service_name="wrangler-tail"}`, because the worker's own OTLP export is not enabled yet.

`data` is Loki's `query_range` response verbatim. Note that `tm.*` attributes arrive as
structured metadata rather than labels, so they are filtered with `|` and not matched in
the selector.

200.description: Loki's answer, plus the caps that were applied.

400.description:
Invalid JSON, or `bad_expression` — the expression is empty, longer than 4096
characters, has no stream selector, has one that will not parse, or has one with no
exact matcher on `service_name`, `namespace` or `job`. `message` names which.

post.summary: Run a PromQL query against Mimir
post.description:
`query_range` over Mimir, capped at 7d, or an instant query with `instant: true`.

**The step is raised, not refused.** A step below `range/1000` is raised to that minimum and
`step_raised: true` says so: the operator asked for a resolution, not for a particular
number of points, and Prometheus refuses more than ~11k points per series anyway.

**The series cap is applied to the answer, not the question.** Mimir has already done the
work by the time the count is known, so the response carries the true `series` count and
`series_truncated: true` alongside the first 200. Shipping 10k series to a browser panel is
what actually breaks the console, which is why the cap is here and not a refusal.

Two metric families named in the dashboards have no data in Mimir today and will come back
as a successful empty result: `tm_provider_build_jobs_total` (use the
`tm_provider_build_duration_seconds_count` histogram instead) and
`http_server_request_duration_seconds_*` (worker HTTP metrics; the worker's OTLP export is
not enabled). An empty result here is an answer, not a failure — a failure is a 5xx.

200.description: Mimir's answer, plus the caps that were applied.

400.description: Invalid JSON, or an empty or over-long expression.

post.summary: Run a TraceQL search against Tempo
post.description:
TraceQL search over Tempo, capped at 24h and 50 results. `data` is Tempo's `/api/search`
response verbatim.

200.description: Tempo's answer, plus the caps that were applied.

400.description: Invalid JSON, or an empty or over-long expression.

get.description:
One trace from Tempo. A completed trace is immutable, so this caches for ten minutes.

`404 not_found` means Tempo holds no trace with that id — most often because it aged out
(14d retention), which is why the message says so rather than reporting an empty trace.
`400 bad_trace_id` means the id is not hex, or is longer than 32 characters: the id is part
of the upstream path, so it is validated against the allowlist pattern before any call.

parameters.name: traceId
parameters.description: Hex trace id, up to 128 bits.

400.description: `bad_trace_id` — the id is not on the allowlist pattern.

404.description: Tempo holds no trace with that id; it may have aged out.

get.summary: List label names for a datasource
get.description:
Label names, for the query console's pickers. Caches for 60s.

Tempo is not a valid `source` here: its equivalent is `/api/v2/search/tags`, whose shape is
different enough that it is not worth pretending otherwise.

400.description: `source` is missing or is not `loki` or `mimir`.

get.summary: List the values of one label
get.description:
The values of one label. Caches for 60s. `name` must match `[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*`: it is
part of the upstream path, so a name outside that pattern is refused by the allowlist
before any call, with 400 `bad_label`.

400.description: `source` is wrong, or `bad_label` — the name is not on the allowlist pattern.

get.summary: The trace and logs for one build, scan or plan
get.description:
One unit of work's telemetry, joined by `journey.id`. The id is the D1 row id — the same
value on a span's `journey.id` and in a log line's `journey_id` — so one id reaches the
trace and the logs with no mapping table.

**The window comes from the row, not from the caller.** A build that ran for an hour three
days ago needs that hour. `build` reads `provider_build_jobs` (`triggered_at` to
`completed_at`), `plan` reads `plan_versions`, and `scan` tries `scan_attempts` first then
`provider_scan_jobs` — module, state and plan scans live in the former and provider scans
in the latter, and both are "a scan" to an operator. A row still running is windowed to
now. `plan_versions` records only `created_at`, so a plan's window end is assumed (one
hour), not known. The window is padded 60s before and 5min after, because telemetry lands
slightly after the row's own timestamps.

**`outside_retention` is not emptiness.** When the window predates what a backend still
holds (Tempo 14d, Loki 30d) that backend is not queried and its part reports
`outside_retention`. An empty result would say "this build produced no telemetry" while
meaning "this build is older than Tempo keeps", and an operator chasing an old failure
needs to know which.

Each part carries its own `status`: `ok`, `outside_retention`, `refused` (the allowlist) or
`error` (with `reason`). One backend failing does not fail the response — the other half is
still worth having.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The D1 row id, which is also the journey id.

200.description: The journey's window, queries, trace and logs.

400.description: `kind` is not `build`, `scan` or `plan`.

404.description: No row of that kind with that id.

get.description:
Every tenant (orgs and personal tenants), newest first, keyset-paginated over
`(created_at, id)`. Pass the returned `next_cursor` back as `cursor` for the next page;
`null` means this is the last page.

Hidden unless asked for: the shared demo org(s) (`demo=1`), because their traffic is not a
customer's, and soft-deleted orgs (`deleted=1`, or `deleted=only` for just the ones
awaiting purge).

`tier` filters on the EFFECTIVE tier: personal tenants always report `starter`, as
`GET /api/orgs` does, whatever the stored column says.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring of the name or slug, or an exact tenant id.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: `org`, `personal`, or `all` (default).

parameters.name: demo
parameters.description: `1` or `true` includes demo orgs.

parameters.name: deleted
parameters.description: `1` or `true` includes soft-deleted orgs; `only` returns nothing else.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Opaque; the `next_cursor` of the previous page.

400.description: A filter value is not recognised, `limit` is out of range, or `cursor` was not issued by this endpoint.

get.summary: Platform-wide daily usage and the busiest tenants
get.description:
Daily totals across every tenant for the same five series as the per-tenant usage
endpoint, plus the ten tenants with the most downloads in the window.

**Demo tenants are excluded by default** (`demo=1` includes them): the shared demo org's
traffic is ours, not a customer's, and would otherwise dominate the top-tenants list.
Soft-deleted tenants are INCLUDED, because their events happened.

A tenant's `downloads` is module downloads of its own modules plus provider downloads
served to it: the same attribution as `GET /api/platform/tenants/{tenantId}/usage`, so the
two agree for any one tenant.

Series are sparse and windowed exactly as described on the per-tenant endpoint.

parameters.name: demo
parameters.description: `1` or `true` includes demo tenants in the series and the top-tenants list.

200.description: The platform's usage in the window.

400.description: `days` is not 30, 90 or 365.

get.summary: One tenant's settings, members, usage and storage
get.description:
Returned for demo and soft-deleted tenants too; they are flagged rather than hidden.

`purge_due_at` is `deleted_at` + 30 days: the date promised in the org-deleted email. No
purge job runs yet, so it is when the promise falls due, not a scheduled event.

Provider downloads come from `provider_download_events`, which is retention-pruned
(400 days), so `provider_downloads_total` is "within retention", not lifetime.
`last_audit_event_at` is `null` for Starter tenants, which write no tenant audit events.

get.summary: One tenant's daily usage, top modules and providers, and storage
get.description:
Daily counts over a fixed window for five series, plus breakdowns over the same window.
Answers for demo and soft-deleted tenants too.

**Window.** `days` buckets of one UTC day each, ending today (UTC). `window.since` is the
UTC midnight that opens the first bucket, so `days=30` covers today and the 29 days
before it, not a rolling 30x24h.

**Sparse series.** Each series lists only the days that had at least one event. A day
that is absent had ZERO events; clients zero-fill onto the `window.from`..`window.to`
domain rather than drawing a line straight across the gap.

**Attribution.**
- `module_downloads`: downloads of this tenant's OWN modules, by anyone.
- `provider_downloads`: provider binaries served TO this tenant.
- `state_pushes`, `plan_uploads`: state and plan versions in the tenant's workspaces.
- `module_publishes`: versions of the tenant's modules, by publish time, any status.

**Retention.** Both download tables are pruned at 400 days, longer than the widest
window, so every window is complete. The version tables count rows still retained: a
state version deleted since its push is not counted.

`storage` is the same per-domain object the tenant detail returns (`null`
`measured_bytes` = unmeasured, never 0 B).

200.description: The tenant's usage in the window.

400.description: `days` is not 30, 90 or 365.

get.description:
Answers `200` only for an admitted platform operator. The portal shows its Admin button
from the token's `roles` claim alone; the console's guard then calls this, so it can tell
"the token has the role" apart from "the worker admits this account" — a `403` here with a
role-bearing token means the account is not on the operator allowlist (or the token was
issued to another client).

200.description: The operator identity as the worker resolved it.

get.description:
The org-wide policy decision ledger (migration 127), newest first: every refusal a policy
caused, and every human override that lifted one.

**Why this is not derivable from the verdict tables.** `policy_results`,
`state_policy_results`, `provider_policy_results` and `plan_policy_results` are all
latest-verdict upserts keyed `(version, policy)` — a re-scan overwrites what the previous
evaluation decided, so they cannot answer "what did the gate tell terraform at 14:03".
These rows never move.

**Passes are not in here.** A successful evaluation is a Prometheus counter
(`tm.plan.gate.evaluations`, `tm.artefact.downloads`), so nothing is written on a served
`terraform init` and the download path takes no write at all. Use `/coverage` for how much
a policy currently passes.

`totals` always covers `window_days` regardless of the row filters, so the header counts do
not move when the list is narrowed.

parameters.name: interaction
parameters.description: Restrict to one interaction.

parameters.name: policy_id
parameters.description: Restrict to decisions caused by one policy.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Unix ms lower bound on `decided_at`. Defaults to the 30-day window.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Case-insensitive substring match over `subject_label`, `reason` and `policy_name`.
`policy_name` is included deliberately: it is denormalised, so a rule that has since
been DELETED is still findable by name. `%` and `_` are escaped, so they match
literally rather than as LIKE wildcards. Longer input is truncated, not rejected.

parameters.name: req_id
parameters.description:
One request's refusal — every row a single `terraform`/`tofu` call produced, which is
one per failing policy.

This is what the terminal prints. A policy-refused state LOCK answers `423` carrying a
synthetic terraform `LockInfo` whose `ID` is `POLICY-BLOCK-<req_id>`, and whose `Info`
links here, so the operator reaches the decision that stopped their apply without
having to search the feed. A leading `POLICY-BLOCK-` is stripped, so pasting the whole
`ID` from the terminal works as well as following the link.

Windowed like every other filter: a link older than `window_days` returns an empty
feed. That is expiry rather than "no such refusal", and the portal says so.

get.summary: Get per-policy coverage and block history
get.description:
For each policy in the org: how many artefact versions its latest stored verdict passes and
fails (current coverage), plus how many refusals it has actually caused in the window.

**Coverage is a count, not a time series, and that is a constraint rather than a choice.**
A per-tenant pass-rate series would have to come from `tm.plan.gate.evaluations` in Mimir,
and cannot: `lib/metrics.ts` excludes `tenant.id` from every metric deliberately (the tenant
count is unbounded) and the collector gateway strips it as a second line of defence. Its own
comment points at the alternative — "per-tenant analysis comes from traces or from D1, which
already holds the authoritative counters" — which is what this endpoint reads.

get.summary: Get the policy input JSON Schema
get.description:
The JSON Schema for the `input` document a Rego policy is evaluated against, for every
artefact kind. Generated from the Worker's own types, so it is the authority for policy
authors — not a restatement.

Pure documentation with no tenant data, so it is unauthenticated and cacheable (5 minutes).
It powers the `?` helper in the Rego editor and the integration guide.

get.summary: Get one artefact's policy input schema
get.description:
A self-contained schema for one artefact kind's `input` — no cross-references to resolve,
so an editor can load just the shape it needs.

404.description: Unknown artefact kind, or no schema available for it.

get.summary: Get policy enablement and blocked counts
get.description:
The enablement snapshot plus how much is currently blocked, which is what makes a toggle
safe to flip: an admin can see the blast radius before enabling enforcement.

`opaTier` is the tier gate. Enforcement needs it **and** the relevant toggle, so
`global: true` with `opaTier: false` evaluates and reports but blocks nothing.

patch.description:
Flips the global master switch, the per-artefact switches, and the missing-signal gate.
Send only the keys you are changing.

**Flipping a toggle recomputes consumability across the org and can enqueue rescans.** Two
consequences visible in the response:

- A request that changes nothing is a true no-op: it returns the current state with
  `changed: false` and `rows_changed: 0`, and performs no recompute, rescan or audit write.
- A request that *does* change something is rate limited — a second flip inside the
  cooldown returns `429`. That debounce is why this is `PATCH` with a delta rather than a
  whole-object `PUT`.

`on_missing_signal` decides how a **missing** trust signal is treated: `ignore` fails open,
`hard_fail` fails closed. It is the single most consequential field here.

schema.description: Only the keys present are considered; a key whose value already matches is ignored.

global.description: Master switch. Off ⇒ nothing is enforced for any artefact kind.

failClosed.summary: Treat a missing trust signal as a failure

200.description:
The resulting settings. `changed: false` means the request was a no-op — nothing was
recomputed and nothing was audited.

429.description:
Settings were changed very recently. The cooldown exists because each real change
triggers an org-wide recompute.

example.message: Policy settings were changed very recently; try again shortly.

get.summary: Get the org consumption kill switch
get.description:
Whether the organisation's Danger-zone "block all consumption" switch is armed, per artefact
type. An armed type refuses **every** consume of it for the whole org: module downloads,
provider downloads, or state reads and applies.

This is not the same mechanism as `/policies/settings`. Those toggles decide whether the
policy *engine* enforces; this one refuses consumption outright and deliberately ignores all
three of their gates — the `opa` tier, `global`, and the per-artefact switch. A kill switch
that silently did nothing because the org was on Starter, or had never turned the policy
feature on, would be a safety bug.

Each artefact type is backed by one row in `policies` flagged `is_block_all`, which is what
gives a refusal a policy name in the decision ledger. That row's Rego is stored for display
only and is never evaluated by OPA or by a scanner — enforcement happens on the serve path,
so arming and disarming both take effect immediately and need no rescan.

`policy_id` is non-null once the switch has *ever* been armed for that artefact: disarming
keeps the row so historical ledger rows still resolve to a policy. `changed_at` and
`changed_by` are only meaningful while `blocked` is true — once disarmed they describe when
it was turned **off**.

There is no stored master flag. `all_blocked` is derived: true when all three are armed.

200.description: The current state of the switch.

403.description: Not an admin of this org.

patch.summary: Arm or disarm the org consumption kill switch
patch.description:
**Owner-only, and humans only** — unlike every other operation in this router, which admits
admins and OIDC bots. Arming this breaks every `terraform init` and `terraform apply` in the
organisation; disarming it removes that protection mid-incident. Neither decision belongs to
a bot token or to an admin.

Send only the keys you are changing. `all` applies one value to every artefact type at once
(what the UI's master switch sends); an explicit per-artefact key in the same request wins
over it. A request that changes nothing returns the current state with an empty `changed`
array and writes no audit event.

**What a refusal looks like to a client.** Status codes differ per artefact, deliberately:

| Surface | Status | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Module download, module archive | `403` | The registry protocol surfaces the detail text. |
| Provider versions list, download metadata, provider files | `404` | This router's convention: a provider the org does not serve must not advertise that it exists. |
| State `LOCK` | `423` | Matches every other state-policy refusal, so an apply fails the way operators already recognise. |
| State read (`GET /state/{org}/*`) | `403` | `423 Locked` would be a lie about a read. |

**It outranks every per-artefact allowance.** `module_versions.consumable_override`, a
module's `serve_override: 'allow'`, and a workspace's `serve_override: 'allow'` are all
ignored while the switch is armed — an owner who armed it meant every artefact, not every
artefact that has not been excused. The one thing still checked first is the platform
blocklist, which is not the org's decision to make.

**One gap, by design.** A provider file URL that was already pre-signed before the switch
was armed keeps resolving until it expires: the signed leg carries no org, so there is
nothing to look the switch up against. This is the same asymmetry pre-signed URLs already
have with entitlement.

Every refusal is written to the decision ledger with `source: block_all` and the backing
policy's id and name, so `/policies/decisions` answers "what did the kill switch stop".

schema.description:
Only the keys present are considered. At least one of `all`, `module`, `provider`
or `state` is required; a body with none of them is a `400` rather than a silent
no-op, because "arm the switch" is not a request to get wrong quietly.

all.description: Apply one value to every artefact type. Applied before the per-artefact keys.

armEverything.summary: Stop all consumption for the org

armProvidersOnly.summary: Refuse provider downloads, leave modules and state serving

200.description:
The resulting state. `changed` lists only the artefact types this request actually
flipped — empty means the request was a no-op.

403.description: Not the org owner, or the caller is a bot rather than a human.

404.description: The caller has no user record in this deployment.

get.description:
Filterable by artefact kind. An artefact-scoped read also carries the compliance rollup
(`eval_failing`, `eval_total`, `eval_failing_names`) so the list can show what each policy
is currently blocking without a second call; an unscoped read omits it.

post.summary: Create a policy
post.description:
The Rego **must** declare `package terramantle.policy` — the evaluator looks for its rules
there, so a different package would silently never fire. That is rejected at `400` rather
than accepted and ignored.

`artefact_type` is validated against the known kinds rather than coerced, so a typo cannot
file a policy under the wrong tab. Leaving it out defaults to `module`.

`instance_key` decides the policy's reach:

- absent ⇒ an **org baseline**, applying to every artefact of that kind and inheritable;
- set ⇒ **identity-custom**, attached to exactly one artefact identity (a module id, a
  state workspace, a provider, a plan workspace key). `artefact_type` is then required,
  because an instance key means nothing without knowing what kind of instance it names.

A policy created here lands **disabled** (`is_enabled: 0`) whatever `is_enforcing` says:
a hand-authored rule is reviewed before it gates anything, and `POST .../toggle` is what
makes it live. The baseline path is the deliberate exception.

Creating a policy enqueues a bundle rebuild for the org.

is_enforcing.description:
Defaults to **`true`**. `false` records verdicts without blocking anything
(advisory). Enforcing requires a tier with OPA enforcement, so `true` on a
plan without it is `403` rather than a silently advisory policy.

instance_key.description: Set for an identity-custom policy. Requires `artefact_type`.

value.name: no-public-ingress

400.description:
Missing `name`/`rego`, a Rego body that does not declare `package terramantle.policy`,
an unknown `artefact_type`, or an `instance_key` with no `artefact_type`.

post.summary: Apply a curated baseline policy set
post.description:
Create several org-baseline policies in one call, **already enabled** — the one path that
does. Everything else lands a policy disabled for review; a baseline set is picked
precisely so it starts working, and an org that has to enable five policies by hand
enables none.

A policy whose name already exists for that artefact is **skipped, never overwritten**,
and reported in `skipped`. The match is on the trimmed, case-folded name against existing
org-baseline policies (`instance_key IS NULL`), which is what makes it catch an org
carrying the same rule under different capitalisation. The point is an org that took a
baseline policy and edited it keeps its own version — so a repeat apply is a no-op rather
than a reset, and the dialog can mark those cards "already exists" before you press
anything. The same folded guard is repeated inside each INSERT, so a double-submit
creates one row, not two.

Admin + human-only, unlike `createPolicy` (`member`): this switches enforcement on across
several artefacts at once, which is the company the other bulk-enforcement routes keep,
and no CI client has a reason to apply a corporate baseline.

`is_enforcing` defaults to `true` and is checked once for the whole call, so on a plan
without OPA enforcement the request is `403` and **nothing** is created. Send
`is_enforcing: false` to apply the same set as advisory.

`rescan` says what happened to the existing artefacts the new policies now cover, and can
only ever describe modules and state: a provider set is re-evaluated at its next
publish/scan, because a provider re-eval is a full clone+scan per version. `queued` means
the fan-out started, `coalesced` that one was triggered within the last hour and this is
folded into it, `none` that nothing needed re-deriving. When `created` is empty — every
card was a duplicate — no bundle rebuild or rescan is triggered at all.

is_enforcing.description: Defaults to `true`. Checked once for the whole call.

policies.description:
At most 25 per request. There is no policy quota, so the batch is bounded
here instead.

crossArtefactBaseline.summary: Modules and providers in one call

policies.name: No critical or high findings
policies.description: Block modules with critical or high severity findings

policies.name: Block malware
policies.description: Block provider builds where the scanner found malware

201.description:
Returned even when every policy was a duplicate and `created` is empty — the request
did what was asked, and the caller reads `created`/`skipped` to say what landed.

reason.description:
The only reason a baseline policy is not created, and it is not an
error: the org already has one by that name.

400.description:
An empty or oversized `policies` array, an entry missing `name`/`rego`, an unknown
`artefact_type`, or a Rego body that does not declare `package terramantle.policy`.
Validation is all-or-nothing: one bad entry creates none of them, and the message
names the offending policy.

403.description:
Not an admin, a bot or machine client, or `is_enforcing: true` on a plan without OPA
enforcement. Nothing is created in any of those cases.

get.summary: List the policies in force for one artefact identity
get.description:
The effective set for a single artefact — org baselines plus any identity-custom policies —
which is what an artefact's policy tab renders. Both parameters are required: an instance
key means nothing without its artefact kind.

parameters.name: instance_key
parameters.description:
The artefact identity — a module id, a state workspace name, a provider key, or a plan
workspace key, depending on `artefact_type`.

400.description: `artefact_type` or `instance_key` missing.

post.summary: Enable or disable every policy for one artefact identity
post.description:
Bulk switch across all policies affecting one artefact — the "turn this artefact's gate off"
action, rather than toggling each policy by hand. `affected` is how many override rows
changed.

patch.description:
Send only the fields to change. A new `rego` body must still declare
`package terramantle.policy`.

The response carries `rescan` alongside the policy: changing a policy means existing
artefacts' verdicts are stale, so the Worker coalesces and enqueues the re-evaluation and
tells you what it queued. A policy edit is never silently retroactive-but-unapplied.

200.description: Updated, with what was queued for re-evaluation.

delete.description:
Removes the policy and its verdicts, and enqueues a bundle rebuild. Artefacts blocked only
by this policy become consumable again once re-evaluated.

post.summary: Toggle a policy on or off
post.description:
Flips `is_enabled`. Returns the policy and the re-evaluation that was queued, as `PATCH`
does.

post.summary: Toggle a policy between advisory and enforcing
post.description:
Flips `is_enforcing` — the difference between a verdict that reports and one that refuses a
download, a provider serve or an apply. The highest-consequence switch on a policy, which
is why it is its own operation rather than a field on a general update.

put.summary: Override one policy for one artefact identity
put.description:
Per-instance control: inherit the org baseline, or pin this artefact's `disabled` /
`enforcing` independently of it. `inherit: true` clears the override and restores the
baseline.

inherit.description: `true` clears the override and restores the org baseline.

post.summary: Force every instance of a policy back to one enforcement level
post.description:
Clears per-instance divergence by setting every instance of this policy to `advisory` or
`enforcing`. The way out of a long tail of hand-made exceptions.

get.description:
The provider catalog: every artefact the org manages, with serve mode, constraint,
resolved source repository, blast radius (which workspaces lock it, which modules declare
it), rolling download windows, cached repository-health stats, and build/patch counts.

Every enrichment is **fault-isolated**. A failing usage, references, downloads, source-URL
or VCS-stats query degrades that column to zero or `null` for the affected rows — it never
takes the list down. So a zero here can mean "none" or "the enrichment was unavailable",
and the list is not the place to assert an absence from.

`patched_count` is a remediation claim and is therefore tier-gated: it reads `0` below the
tier that includes patched builds, even where builds exist.

post.summary: Add a provider to the catalog
post.description:
Adds a provider by hand, populates its version list from upstream, and enqueues the first
scans inline — one call, one managed provider.

`upstream` is **required**: it is part of the artefact's identity and there is no safe
default for an org that may hold both registries. An omitted `version_constraint` means
every version.

Open to every tier, because curating a provider set is not a paid capability. Whether the
org's registry *serves* it is: below that tier the row lands in `serve_mode: off` —
configuration kept, nothing advertised — rather than failing the add.

`409` only if this org already holds the row for **this** registry; the same provider from
the other registry is a separate artefact. Changing an existing row is `PATCH`.

version_constraint.description: Terraform constraint expression. Omitted or empty means all versions.

409.description: The org already manages this provider from this registry.

get.summary: Get a managed provider and its versions
get.description:
Artefact detail plus every version, each annotated with `servable` — the authorization
contract in one boolean: the bytes exist, the version satisfies the org's constraint, and
the org is entitled to it.

A version is only listed once it has a **completed scan**. An unverified version is not
hidden by accident: it is excluded on purpose, and an in-flight build appears under
`GET /api/orgs/{orgId}/provider-flows` as pipeline state instead. That keeps "a version you
can consume" and "work in progress" from ever being the same list.

`downloads.series_90d` is server-capped to the top six versions plus an `other` bucket.
`vcs_stats` is served from cache and is never a live call on this path; `null` means no
resolvable repository or a cache row the scheduled refresh has not filled yet.

400.description: Unknown `upstream`.

patch.summary: Update a provider's constraint or serve mode
patch.description:
Partial update — an omitted field keeps its current value.

**`upstream` in the body is rejected with `400`.** The registry is the artefact's identity;
to serve the same provider from the other registry, add it again from there.

A constraint that genuinely differs from the stored value re-enqueues a scan, because a new
constraint can resolve to versions never scanned. A `serve_mode`-only change never scans,
and never touches `version_constraint`.

`serve_mode: serve` is tier-gated and answers `402` below that tier; `off` and `block` are
open to every tier.

schema.description: At least one field must be present.

400.description:
No fields to update, an invalid `serve_mode`, an unparseable `version_constraint`, or
`upstream` present in the body.

delete.summary: Remove a provider from the catalog
delete.description:
Disassociates the provider from this org. Scan results are **not** deleted — they live in a
cross-org cache keyed by provider version, so other orgs keep theirs and re-adding does not
re-scan from scratch.

The org's registry stops answering for it immediately. May refuse when something still
depends on the row.

409.description: Something still depends on this artefact.

post.summary: Re-scan a provider
post.description:
Enqueues a scan. With no body, the artefact's matching versions; with `version`, just that
one — and if that version names a published patched revision, its patched tree is what gets
scanned.

`200` with `status: "inflight"` means a scan for this provider is already running and
nothing new was queued. That is a success, not a conflict: the work the caller wanted is
already happening.

version.description: Scan only this version. Omit for every matching version.

200.description: A scan is already in progress; nothing new was queued.

example.message: A scan for this provider is already in progress

404.description: No such provider, or no published patched revision for the named version.

post.summary: Refresh a provider's repository-health stats
post.description:
Forces a live fetch of stars, commit activity and latest release from the source
repository, updating the cache the read paths use. Normally a scheduled job; this is the
manual nudge.

200.description: Refreshed. The body reports what was fetched or why it was skipped.

get.summary: Get a download URL for a version's SBOM
get.description:
Returns a short-lived presigned URL rather than the bytes — an SBOM is multi-megabyte SPDX
and the Worker never buffers it.

Authorization happens **before** the URL is minted: the org must manage this
`namespace/type`, the same reader gate the detail read uses. `503` means object-storage
credentials are unconfigured, which is an operator problem rather than a client one.

404.description: No such provider, or no SBOM for this version.

get.summary: Compare an upstream version with its patched revision
get.description:
The finding-level diff between the upstream base version and the newest published patched
revision: what the patch **fixed**, what **remains**, and anything it **introduced** —
plus the major-version bumps that were report-only, and the provenance of the patch (fork
repository, tag, both commit SHAs, the diff URL, any toolchain bump).

That provenance is the point: a patched binary is only trustworthy if you can see exactly
which commits produced it.

Fetched on demand when the comparison panel is expanded, so the detail payload stays light.
